title: LONGEVITY SURVIVOR v2 — Developmental Permission Matrix
frozen_question: Which safety gates change together when mammalian tissues transition from high-fidelity regeneration toward limited repair or fibrosis, and which adult-regenerative tissues retain or transiently reopen those gates?
claim_ceiling: This artifact ranks comparative developmental mechanisms; it does not establish a human rejuvenation therapy.
A repeated pathway across tissues is a candidate shared control node, not proof of one universal regeneration switch.
Direction of a pathway can be cell-type- and time-dependent; YAP and TGF-beta are explicitly not treated as scalar ON/OFF switches.
Mouse neonatal timing is not assumed to map directly to human chronological timing.

topa_result.name: MATURATION_LOCK
topa_result.definition: A coupled transition in which intrinsic cellular plasticity decreases while the tissue niche, immune response, mechanics and repair program mature toward rapid stabilization and scar-biased healing.
topa_result.important_nuance: The lock is a state vector, not a single molecule and not necessarily synchronized to the same postnatal day in every tissue.

maturation_lock_modules.name: PLASTICITY_AND_MITOTIC_COMPETENCE_LOCK
maturation_lock_modules.summary: Across multiple neonatal tissues, regenerative loss tracks reduced ability of differentiated or supporting/progenitor cells to proliferate, transdifferentiate or re-enter a developmental program.
examples: Heart: neonatal cardiomyocyte proliferation is rapidly lost after birth as cardiomyocytes mature, withdraw from the cell cycle, become structurally specialized and often polyploid/binucleated.
Cochlea: neonatal supporting-cell plasticity is largely lost during the first postnatal week; hair-cell enhancers lose a primed chromatin state and become less accessible.
Brain/spinal cord: neonatal neural progenitor proliferative capacity and axon-permissive repair decline with age.
Dense connective tissue: neonatal healing recruits resident and non-resident tenogenic cells more effectively than adult scar-biased healing.

maturation_lock_modules.name: NICHE_AND_MECHANICAL_MATURATION_LOCK
maturation_lock_modules.summary: ECM composition, crosslinking, stiffness and mechanical loading change during maturation and can causally redirect cell behavior toward maturation or fibrosis rather than regeneration.
examples: Heart: postnatal cardiac ECM stiffens rapidly; manipulating crosslinking/stiffness can alter the regenerative window and YAP-associated cardiomyocyte behavior.
Skin: mechanical tension activates a YAP-to-Engrailed-1 fibrotic fibroblast program; blocking this route in mouse wounds can restore appendage-rich regenerative healing.
Spinal cord: neonatal microglia build a transient fibronectin bridge and resolve inflammation, whereas adult lesions form a different scar environment.
Acomys: multiple adult tissues show unusual biomechanics and reduced fibrotic ECM responses together with enhanced regeneration.

maturation_lock_modules.name: IMMUNE_KINETICS_AND_RESOLUTION_LOCK
maturation_lock_modules.summary: Regeneration is not simply low inflammation; it repeatedly requires a correctly timed immune response that clears damage, supports progenitors and then resolves. Adult or non-regenerative states often show altered macrophage/microglial composition, duration or pro-fibrotic signaling.
examples: Heart: neonatal macrophages are required for regeneration and angiogenesis; depletion converts the outcome toward fibrosis.
Spinal cord: neonatal microglia are required for scar-free repair and express inflammation-resolving programs absent from adult microglia.
Tendon: macrophage depletion impairs neonatal functional regeneration.
Fetal skin: scarless healing correlates with shorter/lower inflammatory signaling and distinct TGF-beta isoform balance.
Acomys: reduced pro-inflammatory/fibrotic responses recur across skin, muscle, kidney and spinal cord while macrophages remain necessary for regeneration.

maturation_lock_modules.name: SCAR_PRIORITY_ROUTING_LOCK
maturation_lock_modules.summary: Mature mammalian injury responses often prioritize fast closure and mechanical stability through fibroblast/myofibroblast activation and ECM deposition. Regeneration requires this program to be transient, spatially limited, or actively resolved rather than absent.
examples: Fetal skin transitions from scarless restoration to later scar-forming repair as fibroblast, immune and ECM states mature.
Adult skin mechanotransduction can convert fibroblasts into a scar-producing state through YAP/En1.
Acomys still activates myofibroblasts, but their activation is transient and coupled to blastema/regenerative progression rather than persistent fibrosis.
Liver and lung literature similarly distinguishes transient repair matrix from persistent pathological fibrosis.

context_dependent_nodes_not_master_switc.why: Transient YAP/TAZ activity supports fetal-like reprogramming and regeneration in intestine and can promote cardiomyocyte proliferation, but mechanical YAP in conventional skin fibroblasts can drive En1-positive scar formation. Adult Acomys shows yet another YAP dynamic associated with regeneration.
context_dependent_nodes_not_master_switc.rule: YAP_STATE must include cell_type + upstream mechanical/biochemical context + duration + downstream transcriptional partner.

context_dependent_nodes_not_master_switc.why: TGF-beta1/2-rich persistent signaling is strongly associated with fibrotic adult skin, yet canonical TGF-beta signaling is required for tenocyte recruitment and functional neonatal tendon regeneration; TGF-beta3 is enriched in regenerative contexts.
context_dependent_nodes_not_master_switc.rule: Never encode TGF-beta as simply pro-fibrotic or anti-regenerative without isoform, cell type, amplitude and timing.

context_dependent_nodes_not_master_switc.why: In intestinal injury, p53 is required to terminate a transient fetal-like regenerative state; loss of p53 leaves cells locked in a highly proliferative YAP-high/glycolytic regenerative state and links regenerative persistence to cancer risk.
context_dependent_nodes_not_master_switc.rule: Safe renewal requires both ENTRY and EXIT gates.

tissue_matrix.loss_or_restriction: rapidly postnatal; exact window varies by injury model, commonly within the first week in mouse
gate_changes: oxidative metabolic shift and ROS/DNA-damage signaling
loss of transient fibronectin bridge program
adult scar environment and axon-growth restriction

tissue_matrix.loss_or_restriction: during fetal-to-late-development maturation rather than one universal postnatal date
gate_changes: mechanical tension and YAP-En1 scar routing

adult_regenerative_positive_controls.finding: Adult injury can transiently reactivate fetal-like programs through YAP/TAZ-associated plasticity; p53 is required for exit and restoration of homeostasis.
adult_regenerative_positive_controls.lesson: A mature tissue can retain a reversible developmental permission window if activation and termination remain coupled.

adult_regenerative_positive_controls.finding: Mature differentiated cells can enter paligenosis: autophagy/mTORC1-downshift, state remodeling, then mTORC1 reactivation and cell-cycle re-entry.
adult_regenerative_positive_controls.lesson: Terminal differentiation does not always mean irreversible loss of plasticity; safe regeneration may require staged dismantling and rebuild rather than a single proliferation trigger.

adult_regenerative_positive_controls.finding: Adult liver retains exceptional regeneration through hepatocyte proliferation, dedifferentiation/progenitor activation, immune-ECM coordination and termination signals.
adult_regenerative_positive_controls.lesson: The adult mammal already contains a working example of high regeneration with cancer/fibrosis brakes; it is a critical control, not an exception to ignore.

adult_regenerative_positive_controls.finding: Adult regeneration is preserved through quiescent satellite cells that transiently activate, proliferate, differentiate and self-renew; aging degrades the niche through inflammation, ECM stiffening and altered signaling.
adult_regenerative_positive_controls.lesson: Quiescence itself is not the enemy; reversible quiescence with a preserved niche is a safe-renewal architecture.

adult_regenerative_positive_controls.finding: Adult spiny mice preserve regenerative or low-fibrosis responses across skin, muscle, kidney, heart and spinal cord, with recurring differences in inflammation, biomechanics, cell-cycle deployment and transient fibrotic signaling.
adult_regenerative_positive_controls.lesson: Adult mammalian regeneration is biologically possible without globally remaining neonatal; mature systems can evolve alternative routing of the same injury-response machinery.

reverse_to_human_result.old_question: Which regeneration genes are humans missing?
reverse_to_human_result.new_question: Which coupled maturation locks prevent adult human tissues from transiently entering and then safely exiting a developmental-like regenerative state?

longgevity_survivor_v2.statement: The repeated cross-tissue unit is not permanent youth or unrestricted proliferation. It is reversible developmental plasticity embedded inside a mature safety architecture: enter locally, rebuild, preserve lineage and geometry, suppress malignant escape, then terminate the regenerative state and return to homeostasis.
longgevity_survivor_v2.formula: SAFE_RENEWAL = LOCAL_ENTRY_PERMISSION + PLASTICITY/PROLIFERATION + PERMISSIVE_NICHE + IMMUNE_RESOLUTION + PATTERN_CONTROL + CANCER_GATES + RELIABLE_EXIT
longgevity_survivor_v2.strongest_new_prediction: Adult regenerative tissues and regenerative mammals should differ from scar-biased tissues less by possession of unique genes than by the timing, reversibility and coupling of common developmental, mechanical, immune and termination programs.

next_killer_tests.test: Build a time-aligned multi-tissue matrix (developmental age normalized to regenerative-window closure, not chronological day) for heart, cochlea, spinal cord, tendon and skin; score chromatin accessibility, proliferative competence, ECM stiffness/crosslinking, macrophage/microglia state and fibrotic output at pre-closure, transition and post-closure states.
Use adult-regenerative controls (intestine, liver, skeletal muscle) to identify which MATURATION_LOCK modules are transiently reopened after injury and which remain permanently open.

Compare ordinary mouse versus adult Acomys across matched tissues to test whether reduced fibrosis and regenerative healing co-segregate with immune-resolution kinetics and ECM/mechanotransduction rather than a single pathway.

Search for a conserved ENTRY/EXIT pair: candidate ENTRY nodes include YAP/TAZ-fetal-like reversion and paligenosis; candidate EXIT nodes include p53-dependent termination, restoration of Wnt/RA/homeostatic programs and re-establishment of quiescence.
